item.text:
Rain begins when water from oceans, lakes, rivers, and damp ground evaporates. Heat from the Sun turns some liquid water into invisible water vapor, which rises into the air. Plants also release water vapor through their leaves, adding moisture to the atmosphere.

As moist air rises, it expands because the air pressure around it decreases. Expanding air cools. When it cools enough, it reaches a temperature called the dew point, at which water vapor can condense. Tiny airborne particles—such as dust, sea salt, or smoke—give the vapor a surface to condense on. The droplets that form around these particles are extremely small, and together they make a cloud.

Cloud droplets do not usually fall as rain right away. They are so tiny that rising air currents can keep them floating. To grow large enough to fall, droplets must gather more water. In warm clouds, droplets collide as they move through the air. Some merge into bigger drops, which then collide with others. This process repeats until the drops become heavy enough for gravity to pull them down.

In colder clouds, ice crystals can help produce precipitation. Water vapor may turn directly into ice crystals, while nearby cloud droplets remain liquid despite being below freezing. The crystals grow as water vapor collects on them, then fall and may join with other crystals to form snowflakes. If they pass through warmer air on the way down, they melt and reach the ground as rain. If they stay frozen, they fall as snow. In some storms, layers of freezing air or strong updrafts can produce sleet or hail instead.

A falling drop does not always make it to the ground. If it passes through a dry layer of air, some or all of it may evaporate. That is why rain can sometimes be seen falling from a cloud but disappearing before it reaches the surface. When the air below the cloud is moist enough, the drops survive their descent.

The size and spacing of raindrops vary. Small drops fall slowly and may drift with the wind, while larger drops descend faster. Very large drops can break apart as air pushes against them. The rain that reaches the ground can soak into soil, flow into streams and rivers, or collect in lakes and oceans. Some of it later evaporates, beginning the cycle again.

Tiny airborne particles—such as dust, sea salt, or smoke—give the vapor a surface to condense on. The droplets that form around these particles are extremely small, and together they make a cloud.

This process repeats until the drops become heavy enough for gravity to pull them down.

As moist air rises, it expands because the air pressure around it decreases. Expanding air cools. When it cools enough, it reaches a temperature called the dew point, at which water vapor can condense. Tiny airborne particles—such as dust, sea salt, or smoke—give the vapor a surface to condense on. The droplets that form around these particles are extremely small, and together they make a cloud.

Cloud droplets do not usually fall as rain right away. They are so tiny that rising air currents can keep them floating. To grow large enough to fall, droplets must gather more water. In warm clouds, droplets collide as they move through the air. Some merge into bigger drops, which then collide with others. This process repeats until the drops become heavy enough for gravity to pull them down.

In colder clouds, ice crystals can help produce precipitation. Water vapor may turn directly into ice crystals, while nearby cloud droplets remain liquid despite being below freezing. The crystals grow as water vapor collects on them, then fall and may join with other crystals to form snowflakes. This process repeats until the drops become heavy enough for gravity to pull them down.

In colder clouds, ice crystals can help produce precipitation. Water vapor may turn directly into ice crystals, while nearby cloud droplets remain liquid despite being below freezing. The crystals grow as water vapor collects on them, then fall and may join with other crystals to form snowflakes. If they pass through warmer air on the way down, they melt and reach the ground as rain. If they stay frozen, they fall as snow. In some storms, layers of freezing air or strong updrafts can produce sleet or hail instead.

Rain begins when water from oceans, lakes, rivers, and damp ground evaporates. Heat from the Sun turns some liquid water into invisible water vapor, which rises into the air. Plants also release water vapor through their leaves, adding moisture to the atmosphere.

As moist air rises, it expands because the air pressure around it decreases. Expanding air cools. When it cools enough, it reaches a temperature called the dew point, at which water vapor can condense. Tiny airborne particles—such as dust, sea salt, or smoke—give the vapor a surface to condense on. The droplets that form around these particles are extremely small, and together they make a cloud.

As moist air rises, it expands because the air pressure around it decreases. Expanding air cools. When it cools enough, it reaches a temperature called the dew point, at which water vapor can condense. Tiny airborne particles—such as dust, sea salt, or smoke—give the vapor a surface to condense on. The droplets that form around these particles are extremely small, and together they make a cloud.

Cloud droplets do not usually fall as rain right away. They are so tiny that rising air currents can keep them floating. To grow large enough to fall, droplets must gather more water. In warm clouds, droplets collide as they move through the air. Some merge into bigger drops, which then collide with others. This process repeats until the drops become heavy enough for gravity to pull them down.

In colder clouds, ice crystals can help produce precipitation. Water vapor may turn directly into ice crystals, while nearby cloud droplets remain liquid despite being below freezing. The crystals grow as water vapor collects on them, then fall and may join with other crystals to form snowflakes. If they pass through warmer air on the way down, they melt and reach the ground as rain. If they stay frozen, they fall as snow. In some storms, layers of freezing air or strong updrafts can produce sleet or hail instead.

A falling drop does not always make it to the ground. If it passes through a dry layer of air, some or all of it may evaporate. That is why rain can sometimes be seen falling from a cloud but disappearing before it reaches the surface. When the air below the cloud is moist enough, the drops survive their descent.
